78.t: Coming to Denver in the 1960s and the Clef Club's beginnings
78.s: Horace moved from California about twelve years earlier, found jam sessions at a Washington Avenue club with Shelly Rhythm and Ron Washington, and bassist Chuck Roberts, then an after-hours club.
78.ch: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
78.q: Yes, I came here from California. I'd heard about the mile high climate and all, and I just had met some people in California, and they said, "You should come to Denver," one of these things, and I said, "Well, the first chance I where time off, that were chance I might get when I get a little free…

78.t: Clef Club finances, the $1,500 rent and hotels paying to keep it closed
78.s: Rent and charter fees ran $1,000 a month covered by $5 memberships; after the win the landlord demanded $1,500 rent, and Horace says six downtown hotels paid him $100,000 each to keep it shut.
78.ch: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
78.q: And we won the case, and I'll inject a little financial thing here. We were paying rent down to an agency here that owned a lot of buildings, Dikreau the building. It's called the Review Realty. He was renting us this place for his -- for $750.00 a month. We were playing -- paying $250.00 a month…

78.t: Running the Clef Club as a nonprofit bottle club
78.s: Horace and his wife ran the after-hours club for a corporation headed by attorney Robert Carr, in the old Arthur Murray studio, a bottle club sponsored by the Rudinsky Foundation, hosting Stan Kenton's birthday.
78.ch: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
78.q: Yes, my wife and I ran that club for the corporation that owned it, and we were part of that corporation. In fact, the gentleman that was president of the corporation was --

78.t: Clef Club's performers, 3,500 members, and its closing by the legislature
78.s: Local nightclub performers played better there after their jobs; with 3,500 members it ran almost three years before the Colorado legislature, under pressure, passed a law closing it.
78.ch: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
78.q: Oh, the performers that would even perform at every nightclub all over the city (unintelligible) would come in after they finished their evening engagement. And they would get up and ask to perform. And they would perform before the other performers. And they would give a greater performance there…

99.t: Swapping bands between the two clubs and the Riviera's decline
99.s: The owners swap Eckstine's band for Pillars's, and cheaper acts and weaker business lead the Riviera to close in 1945.
99.q: To bring our band back to the Plantation, and take his band over to the Club Riviera. And, of course, Billy Eckstine was a big hit over there, because he had just left Earl Hines not too long before that, where he had sung that "you know?" song Jelly Jelly, you know? And so it was mutually agreed…

99.t: Why the Jeter-Pillars band left the Plantation
99.s: After ten years the club replaced the band with big names like Cab Calloway and the Mills Brothers, which Pillars says began its downfall.

99.t: The Club Plantation in Kansas City burns down, 1940
99.s: The band and show open a Kansas City branch whose fancy food and small market fail, and it burns down about the fifth week.
99.q: That's right. We opened up a Club Plantation in Kansas City. They opened up a club in Kansas City, in 1940. And we took the whole show and band up there, the whole Kitchen

178.t: Crowds at the Melody Inn and why it closed
178.s: Musicians and packed crowds came; the owner had a heart attack, sold the place and died, and the band moved to Happy Land.
178.ch: The Melody Inn and the Mighty Four
178.q: Well what happened was that Hyde was ill and then he had a heart attack and so he sold the place to one of his employees and oddly about three weeks after he sold, he dropped

251.t: The Keyhole Club, a failed New Orleans move, and reopening in San Antonio
251.s: Keyhole opened in 1944 and closed in 1948; he lost money in New Orleans and reopened in San Antonio in 1950.
251.ch: Keyhole, comeback plans and old New Orleans players
251.q: and I closed it in 1948 and I thought I wanted to go to New Orleans and open a massive club down there and I sold out everything I had there and went to New Orleans and I found out that the ways of living down there was different from the ideas that I have in regards to nightclub and also to music…

918.t: Tony Alvarez's club closing in New Orleans
918.s: Discussion of a Royal Street club with photographs of the old musicians, which closed because it did not draw.
918.q: You know he don't have that burn that royal street running anymore No Oh is that right? What happens not there? Well I was there and Wynton was close Should have been open but it was close

303.s: Describes the Red Carpet membership club on Common Street, where he met Jim Garrison, and the loan he never got back.
303.ch: New Orleans clubs and Sharky's band
303.q: It was on, on, uh, the first street off of. Common. It's on Common Street, yeah, right across from the old St. Charles Hotel. And, uh. From the side entrance to the old St. Charles Hotel.

938.s: Noto's coffee house and later club, bookings of Chet Baker and others, and the hardships of club ownership.
938.ch: Vegas, clubs and the jazz life
938.q: It’s a hard row to go. People don’t have any idea. The organization of it alone, just booking somebody for one night a week, 52 weeks a year, is a full time job. Incredible.

349.t: Re-establishing himself in New York after Hampton
349.s: Returning to the city was not hard; club owners care about the cash register.
349.q: Back in the City, yeah. Well that wasn’t too hard to do you know, because club owners are funny. All they’re interested in is seeing the cash register ring. As long as the cash register keeps on ringing, most of them, they just go on about their business doing whatever they’re going to do. Some of…

450.s: Investors wanted gambling and red velvet and disrespected her husband, so she left the club; she also recalls introducing acts every night.
450.q: The reason was that the people with the money wanted to tart it up and bring in gambling. I said no. They showed no respect for my husband, Sean. They were starting to book people that was not my taste. They wanted to make it all gold and red velvet. I said, uh-uh, it’s time to go. That’s what I…

80.t: Carey's ritzy Red Garter club fails; Carey as an amateur bassist
80.s: Carey's Red Garter flopped because he drove away neighbourhood customers with dress rules, and he loved playing though not a musician, even imitating Johnny Ray.
80.q: Because -- well, I don't know. He has an idea I think back in his mind he wanted to -- he wanted to have a ritzy -- a ritzy place. I don't know. He didn't want the guys to come in there without a tie on, or in a jacket. He didn't want to serve them, you know, and it's a neighborhood where there…

88.t: Kay Starr's $6,500 ring and the club's closing
88.s: Hal Stanley wanted Kay Starr's ring to keep the club open another week; she refused and the club closed.
88.ch: Own bands and Los Angeles clubs
88.q: As a matter of fact, there's a funny story about it. Hal wanted to keep the place opened one more week, and he had given her an engagement ring that cost $6500, you know? So I was in the office with him this night, and he was saying, 'Kay, you got to let me have the ring, I think if I get off the…

4.t: How Music Town ended and the Wells Fargo building
4.s: Austin McCoy was drafted, returned restless, sold out, and Spikes sold the operation to the Masonic Lodge and went into real estate.
4.ch: Central Avenue clubs, Nordskog, Sheffield and Music Town
4.q: Oh, I stayed up there till...see, Austin got drafted in the Army. He was away two, three years. And then I was there by myself, and when he come back, just like all soldiers--they wild, you know--they been cooped up so long--he didn't want to work, he come in four o'clock in the afternoon. Next day…

93.t: The Hotcha Club declines under a new owner
93.s: Asked about tap's decline, Green describes the old Hotcha Club being run down by a new owner, who left, so dancers lost a place to originate steps.
93.ch: Split, hospital and decline of tap
93.q: This owner, this new owner -- he had bought the old Hacha Not-Shot Club, see, and turned it into a night club -- well, it was like a place of pleasure, see. Like, it had a gaming room, you know, and refreshments, and naturally it was very - how can you say -- I'll say an overwhelming place, you…

29.t: How the old Apex became the Alabam, and the new Apex closed
29.s: Mrs. Howard says Italian owners turned the first Apex into the Alabam and the new Apex closed after a killing there.
29.ch: Reel 2: Los Angeles musicians, the Apex and Cotton Club
29.q: Oh, yes, yes, it was larger than this one, and that's where the Alabam was. You see, after the Apex closed there, then these Italians took it over and named it the Alabam.

388.t: The Famous Door closes and Leeman takes kitchen items
388.s: The club's management tells the band to take what they want before receivership, and Leeman takes pots and a meat cleaver.
388.q: About then, things were slowing down on the street financially for the owners of clubs, and we closed The Famous Door; it was closing after many years. And the management came up and told us, 'Look, we're closing, we can't afford to keep open and so I thought I'd tip you off
